(CNN) -- In the pre-dawn darkness Saturday, long after her parents and brother were asleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay in bed cradling the house phone and her cell phone in her hands. Atefeh Yazdi visits with her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, during his trip to America last year. The only light was from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran, and her laptop displaying her Facebook page in hope of any updates on what was happening halfway around the world. "I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn't see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook," the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. Repeated calls to relatives in Tehran only got the "annoying" Farsi-language error message. She recounted the thoughts running through her brain all night: "Are they going to really shoot people? What's going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?" In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani said the anxiety of waiting and wondering was like endless pacing at a hospital during a loved one's operation. "It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn't ended," Soltani, 28, told CNN by telephone. "I'm worried. I'm hoping it will be good but I'm worried it will get very ugly." The jumble of emotions -- fear, hope, anxiety, frustration -- were reality for millions of Iranian-Americans trying to find out if Iranian authorities would crush protests over last week's election. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in voting that opposition groups called rigged. No independent monitors were permitted for the election. A threatening statement Friday by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei increased fears of bloodshed. Iranian authorities have cut off traditional communications such as cell phone connections, and also banned foreign news outlets from covering the protests. Thousands of protesters took to the streets Saturday, even though the demonstrations were banned and police confronted them with clubs, tear gas and water cannons. The uncertainty and unrest strikes close to home for Yazdi, whose grandfather -- a longtime politician in Iran -- was arrested from his hospital bed this week. He's been returned to the hospital, she said, but she doesn't know if he'll be arrested again or what will happen to other relatives. "It's very exhausting," Yazdi said. "I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don't care about the risks involved." Her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, say such talk is foolish, she said. They are as worried as she is, but fear returning now would bring too much risk. "There's a generation gap, a culture gap," she explained. It runs deep, defining her life as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States, who refers to Iranians as "my people." "Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I'm culturally confused," Yazdi said. "I'm not completely American the right way, and I'm not completely Iranian the right way." Soltani also mentioned the generation gap among Iranian-Americans, but he described it as more political. His parents' generation lost everything in the revolution, and will only consider returning when the revolutionary regime has been toppled, he said. Older Iranian-Americans in the United States "actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you're just legitimizing the government," Soltani said. "We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you're going to the other team," is how Soltani characterized their attitude. "They think the system needs to go completely," he said. "All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they're going to be able to go back." No matter what happens, Soltani and Yazdi said, Iran is changed forever by this week's events. "I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive," Soltani said. "Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they're not going to be able to stop them."

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — In the pre-dawn darkness Saturday, long after her parents and brother had fallen asleep, Atefeh Yazdi lay in bed, cradling the house phone and her cell phone in her hands.

The only light came from a television tuned to the latest news from Iran and a laptop displaying her Facebook page, where she hoped to find updates about events unfolding halfway around the world.

“I kind of felt I was more there when I couldn't see the rest of the room, just the TV and the Facebook,” the 28-year-old Iranian-American told CNN by telephone from her home in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania.

Repeated calls to relatives in Tehran yielded only an “annoying” Farsi-language error message. She recounted the thoughts racing through her mind all night: “Are they going to really shoot people? What's going to happen? Is this going to turn into massive killing and violence?”

In Houston, Texas, Reza Soltani said the anxiety of waiting and wondering felt like endlessly pacing through a hospital while a loved one underwent an operation.

“It feels like the operation started last week and it hasn't ended,” Soltani, 28, told CNN by telephone. “I'm worried. I'm hoping it will be good but I'm worried it will get very ugly.”

That tangle of emotions—fear, hope, anxiety and frustration—was a reality for millions of Iranian-Americans trying to determine whether Iranian authorities would crush protests over the previous week’s election.

President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the overwhelming victor in a vote that opposition groups called rigged. No independent monitors were permitted to observe the election. A threatening statement Friday by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei heightened fears of bloodshed.

Iranian authorities cut off traditional communications, including cell phone connections, and banned foreign news outlets from covering the protests. Thousands of demonstrators nevertheless took to the streets Saturday, despite a ban on the protests, and police confronted them with clubs, tear gas and water cannons.

For Yazdi, the uncertainty and unrest hit especially close to home. Her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, a longtime Iranian politician whom she had visited during his trip to America the previous year, was arrested from his hospital bed that week. He had since been returned to the hospital, she said, but she did not know whether he would be arrested again or what might happen to her other relatives.

“It's very exhausting,” Yazdi said. “I have this feeling I want to be there. I want to book the next flight. I want to be with the people. I don't care about the risks involved.”

Her parents, who left Iran in the 1970s before the Islamic Revolution, considered such talk foolish, she said. They were as worried as she was but feared that returning at that moment would pose too great a risk.

“There's a generation gap, a culture gap,” she explained.

That divide runs deep, shaping her life as an American-born citizen of both Iran and the United States who refers to Iranians as “my people.”

“Being born and raised in America, where I was able to voice my opinion, do what I want, say what I wanted, I'm culturally confused,” Yazdi said. “I'm not completely American the right way, and I'm not completely Iranian the right way.”

Soltani also spoke of a generation gap among Iranian-Americans, though he described it as more political. His parents’ generation lost everything in the revolution and would consider returning only after the revolutionary regime had been toppled, he said.

Older Iranian-Americans in the United States “actually boycotted the election, saying if you vote you're just legitimizing the government,” Soltani said.

“We sacrificed everything for you guys, and now you're going to the other team,” is how Soltani characterized their attitude.

“They think the system needs to go completely,” he said. “All they care is for the system to collapse. They think if the system collapses, they're going to be able to go back.”

Whatever happened, Soltani and Yazdi said, Iran had been changed forever by that week’s events.

“I believe that anything that comes out of it will be positive,” Soltani said. “Even if they fail now, the people know if they get in the streets in millions, they're not going to be able to stop them.”

Her room was illuminated only by a television carrying the latest reports from Iran and a laptop open to Facebook, where she searched for information about events unfolding across the world.

Yazdi, a 28-year-old Iranian American living in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, told CNN by phone that shutting out the rest of the room and focusing solely on the television and Facebook made her feel closer to Iran.

Her repeated attempts to contact family members in Tehran produced only what she described as an irritating recorded error message in Farsi. Throughout the night, she wondered whether authorities would actually fire on demonstrators, what might happen next, and whether the unrest would escalate into widespread violence and killing.

In Houston, Texas, 28-year-old Reza Soltani compared the prolonged uncertainty to pacing through a hospital while someone close to you undergoes surgery—with the procedure seeming to have begun the previous week and still not being over. Speaking to CNN by telephone, he said he hoped the outcome would be positive but feared the situation could become extremely ugly.

Millions of Iranian Americans were experiencing the same mix of hope, fear, frustration and anxiety as they tried to determine whether Iranian officials would violently suppress demonstrations over the election held the week before. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had been announced as the decisive winner, although opposition organizations alleged that the vote had been manipulated. Independent election observers were not allowed.

Concerns about possible bloodshed intensified after Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a warning on Friday. Iranian officials had disrupted conventional means of communication, including cellular phone service, and prohibited foreign news organizations from reporting on the demonstrations.

Despite a ban on protests, thousands of people entered the streets on Saturday. Police confronted them using batons, tear gas and water cannons.

For Yazdi, the turmoil was especially personal. Her grandfather, Dr. Ebrahim Yazdi, a veteran Iranian politician whom she had visited during his trip to the United States the previous year, had been taken into custody from his hospital bed during the week. She said he had since been brought back to the hospital, but she did not know whether he might be arrested again or what could happen to her other family members.

Yazdi described the experience as deeply draining. She said she felt compelled to be in Iran, wanted to take the next available flight and join the people there, regardless of the danger.

According to Yazdi, her parents—who departed Iran during the 1970s, before the Islamic Revolution—considered that idea reckless. Although they shared her concern, they believed traveling back at that moment would be far too dangerous.

She attributed their different reactions to both generational and cultural divides. Those tensions are central to her identity as an American-born citizen of the United States and Iran who calls Iranians “my people.” Yazdi said that growing up in America gave her the freedom to express herself and live as she chose, but also left her culturally divided: she does not feel entirely American in the expected sense or entirely Iranian in the expected sense.

Soltani also identified a divide between generations of Iranian Americans, though he viewed it primarily in political terms. He said members of his parents’ generation lost everything during the revolution and would consider returning only after the revolutionary government was removed.

Many older Iranian Americans in the United States boycotted the election because they believed participation would give legitimacy to the government, Soltani said. He summarized their perspective as resentment that, after sacrificing everything for the younger generation, their children were now appearing to side with the opposing camp.

In his view, those older exiles want the political system dismantled altogether. Their chief concern is seeing it collapse because they believe that would make it possible for them to return to Iran.

Whatever the immediate result, both Yazdi and Soltani believed the week’s developments had permanently transformed Iran. Soltani said he expected something beneficial to emerge from the unrest. Even if the demonstrators did not succeed at that moment, he argued, Iranians had learned that authorities could not stop them if millions gathered in the streets.

Many spent hours following television reports, searching Facebook and other social-media sites, and repeatedly calling relatives and friends in Iran. Because official information was limited and often contradictory, even brief messages, photographs, and videos became vital sources of news.

Communication grew increasingly difficult as Iranian authorities restricted internet access, disrupted mobile-phone service, and limited text messaging. Calls often failed, websites became inaccessible, and messages arrived only after long delays. For families in the United States, the silence was especially distressing. They had no reliable way to know whether loved ones were safe, had joined demonstrations, or had been caught in clashes with security forces.

The government’s restrictions on foreign journalists deepened the uncertainty. With international reporters unable to move freely or cover the protests directly, Iranian citizens took on the role of witnesses. Using mobile phones and social-media platforms, they shared accounts of demonstrations, images of crowds, and evidence of violence. These reports were sometimes difficult to verify, but they offered a rare view of events unfolding beyond the reach of official state media.

Members of the Iranian diaspora responded by circulating updates, translating messages, and drawing international attention to the protesters’ demands. Social media connected people across borders and allowed information to continue flowing despite efforts to suppress it. At the same time, Iranian-Americans worried that those posting material from inside the country could be identified, arrested, or punished.

Reports of arrests and warnings of a harsher crackdown intensified those fears. Every unsuccessful phone call raised the possibility that a relative or friend might be in danger. Yet the scale and persistence of the demonstrations also inspired hope. Many Iranian-Americans saw the protests as evidence that ordinary citizens were willing to demand political accountability and make their voices heard.

For the diaspora, the crisis was therefore both political and deeply personal. It revealed the human cost of repression: families separated by distance, citizens afraid to speak openly, and communities forced to rely on fragments of information. It also demonstrated the growing importance of social media as an information lifeline. Although digital platforms could not eliminate fear or guarantee the truth of every report, they helped citizens bear witness, kept families connected, and prevented a communications blackout from becoming complete silence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Iranian-Americans anxiously following the 2009 post-election protests in Iran, focusing on Atefeh Yazdi and Reza Soltani.
counterfactuals.output:
**Iranian-Americans anxiously watch protests unfold in Iran**

*By Staff Writer*  
*June 2009*

For Atefeh Yazdi, the images arriving from Iran are difficult to watch—and impossible to ignore.

Like many Iranian-Americans, Yazdi has spent the days since Iran’s disputed presidential election moving between television reports, online videos and messages from friends and relatives. Each new image of demonstrators filling Tehran’s streets brings hope that Iranians are making their voices heard. Each report of gunfire, arrests or injured protesters brings renewed fear.

Reza Soltani is following the unrest with the same anxious intensity. Thousands of miles from Iran, he watches a political crisis unfold through shaky cellphone footage, social-media posts and fragmented news reports—often without knowing whether the people he cares about are safe.

Their experience reflects the uncertainty gripping much of the Iranian diaspora after election officials declared President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the overwhelming winner of the June 12 vote. Opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi and his supporters challenged the result, alleging widespread irregularities and demanding a new election.

Iranian authorities rejected those claims and moved to contain the protests. Foreign journalists faced restrictions, websites were blocked and mobile-phone service was disrupted. As the flow of verified information narrowed, Iranians inside the country increasingly turned to Twitter, Facebook, YouTube and e-mail to document demonstrations and the government’s response.

For Yazdi and Soltani, those digital fragments have become both a lifeline and a source of distress.

A brief message can offer reassurance. A long silence can trigger hours of worry. Graphic videos—some showing bloodied demonstrators or security forces confronting crowds—provide a glimpse of what is happening, but often arrive without enough context to confirm where or when they were recorded.

That uncertainty is especially painful for Iranian-Americans who feel closely connected to the country but are physically removed from the events.

Many left Iran years ago or grew up in the United States hearing stories about the country from parents and grandparents. The protests have reopened complicated emotions: pride in the demonstrators, anger over the crackdown, concern for relatives and frustration at being unable to help from afar.

Across the United States, Iranian-Americans have gathered for candlelight vigils and solidarity rallies. Some carry signs asking, “Where is my vote?”—the question that became a rallying cry for Mousavi’s supporters. Others wear green, the color associated with his campaign and the emerging protest movement.

Yet even within the diaspora, views are not uniform. Iranians abroad differ over the candidates, the future of the Islamic Republic and the role the United States should play. Many worry that overt American intervention could allow Iranian leaders to portray the demonstrations as foreign-directed.

The Obama administration has responded cautiously, expressing concern about violence and calling for Iranians’ voices to be heard while stopping short of endorsing a particular political outcome.

For people like Yazdi and Soltani, however, the crisis is more personal than geopolitical.

Behind every crowd shown on television, they see individuals who could be friends, cousins or former classmates. Behind every disruption in communication is the possibility that someone they know has been arrested, hurt or simply cut off from the outside world.

And so they keep watching—refreshing computer screens, checking phones and waiting for the next message from Iran.

The distance offers safety, but little comfort.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a human-interest report on how communications blackouts and political unrest after Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s disputed re-election affected young Iranian-Americans in the United States.
counterfactuals.output:
## Between Two Worlds, Young Iranian-Americans Watched Iran Go Dark

In June 2009, the distance between Tehran and the United States was measured less in miles than in unanswered phone calls.

After Iranian authorities declared President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the winner of a disputed re-election, mass demonstrations spread through Tehran and other cities. Supporters of opposition candidate Mir-Hossein Mousavi filled the streets, demanding to know what had happened to their votes. The government responded with arrests, restrictions on foreign journalists and disruptions to mobile-phone and internet service.

For young Iranian-Americans, many of whom had grown up hearing family stories about revolution, war and exile, the blackout made an already frightening crisis intensely personal. Calls to relatives failed. Text messages disappeared. Social-media accounts went silent without explanation.

A missed call could mean a crowded network. It could also mean that a cousin had joined a march, that an uncle had been detained or simply that a family was afraid to speak.

Across the United States, college students and young professionals stayed awake deep into the night, refreshing Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and Persian-language news sites. They searched shaky cellphone videos for familiar streets and listened closely to voices shouting from rooftops. Because Iran had sharply limited conventional reporting, fragments of information—an anonymous post, a few seconds of video, a message passed through several people—often became the only available evidence of what was happening.

The result was a mixture of urgency and helplessness. Young Iranian-Americans translated Persian messages, reposted demonstrations’ locations and circulated technical advice about proxy servers intended to help Iranians bypass online restrictions. Some changed their profile photographs to green, the color associated with Mousavi’s campaign. Others joined rallies in cities including Los Angeles, New York and Washington, holding signs that read, “Where is my vote?”

But digital activism carried risks. Iranian-Americans worried that identifying protesters or sharing unverified information could expose people inside Iran. Some avoided naming relatives or publishing photographs. Families cautioned younger members that visible activism in the United States might endanger loved ones abroad—or complicate future travel to Iran.

The uncertainty also exposed generational differences. Parents who had experienced the 1979 revolution or later repression sometimes urged restraint. Their children, accustomed to speaking publicly online, often felt compelled to act. For some, the unrest transformed Iranian identity from something expressed mainly through food, music and family gatherings into an immediate political responsibility.

The death of 26-year-old Neda Agha-Soltan, captured on video during the protests, intensified that sense of connection. Her final moments circulated widely online and made the crackdown painfully intimate. To many young people in the diaspora, she did not appear as a distant political symbol but as someone close to their own age—someone who might have been a cousin, classmate or friend.

At the same time, many resisted having Iran reduced to images of violence or to a simple contest between the government and the West. They emphasized that the protesters’ demands came from within Iranian society. Their concern was not merely about American foreign policy; it was about the safety and dignity of people whose language, memories and family histories they shared.

The communications blackout never became absolute. Information continued to escape through intermittent calls, emails, videos and personal networks. Yet the gaps were themselves powerful. Silence forced families to imagine what could not be confirmed, while every brief message—“We are safe,” “Do not call,” “Internet is down”—carried extraordinary weight.

For young Iranian-Americans, the aftermath of the election blurred the boundary between here and there. They were physically safe in American homes, dormitories and offices, but emotionally tethered to streets thousands of miles away. The crisis drew many more deeply into activism and strengthened ties within the diaspora. It also left lasting anxiety about surveillance, censorship and the fragility of contact with family.

When Iran’s networks went dark, young Iranian-Americans tried to fill the silence. They translated, verified, demonstrated and waited. Above all, they kept their phones nearby, hoping that the next call would finally get through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Iranian diaspora watches protests with fear, hope — and frustration from afar

**As relatives in Tehran join banned demonstrations and security forces intensify a crackdown, Iranians abroad are scrambling for information and searching for ways to help.**

For many Iranians living abroad, every message from Tehran now carries two emotions: relief that a loved one is safe, and fear that the next message may never arrive.

Families separated by borders and unreliable internet connections are following the banned demonstrations through brief phone calls, grainy videos and fragmented social media posts. Some say relatives have joined crowds demanding change despite the risk of arrest, injury or worse. Others have urged family members to stay home, even as they share the protesters’ anger.

“I’m proud of them, but I’m terrified,” said **[NAME]**, an Iranian **[profession]** living in **[CITY]**, whose **[relative]** has attended demonstrations in Tehran. “Every time the phone rings, I think something has happened.”

The demonstrations have become a source of renewed hope for parts of the diaspora, many of whom left Iran after earlier waves of unrest or political repression. But that hope is tempered by memories of previous crackdowns, when security forces arrested protesters and authorities restricted communications.

The Iranian government has portrayed unauthorized protests as a threat to public order and has accused foreign governments and media organizations of encouraging unrest. Rights groups and opposition activists, meanwhile, say authorities have responded with intimidation, detentions and force. **[Insert verified casualty and arrest figures, with attribution, if available.]**

Because access for independent journalists is limited and communications are frequently disrupted, many accounts from inside Iran cannot be immediately verified.

For relatives abroad, the information vacuum can be agonizing.

**[NAME]**, who lives in **[COUNTRY]**, said her family in Tehran has begun using coded language during calls. A request to “check on grandmother,” she said, can mean that security forces are nearby. A blank message may be intended only to show that the sender still has access to a phone.

“Sometimes they disappear for hours,” she said. “You don’t know if the internet is down, if their battery is dead or if they have been taken.”

Across diaspora communities, Iranians have organized solidarity rallies, contacted lawmakers, raised money for human rights groups and circulated tools intended to help people bypass online restrictions. Yet many say those efforts feel painfully small compared with the risks being taken inside Iran.

That helplessness has also fueled frustration toward Western governments. Some diaspora activists are calling for stronger diplomatic pressure and targeted sanctions against officials linked to the crackdown. Others worry that broad economic measures could deepen hardship for ordinary Iranians without changing the government’s behavior.

There are divisions within the diaspora as well. Iranians abroad do not always agree on what political change should look like, which opposition figures should be supported or how foreign powers should respond. But many say the immediate priority is protecting demonstrators and keeping Iran connected to the outside world.

“This is not the moment to make it about personalities,” said **[NAME]**, an organizer with **[GROUP]**. “People inside Iran are asking the world not to look away.”

In Tehran, families are making their own calculations. Some protesters leave their phones at home because they fear being tracked. Parents plead with adult children to avoid crowded streets. Others quietly prepare food, medical supplies or a place to sleep for relatives who may be unable to return home.

For those watching from thousands of miles away, daily life continues in uneasy contrast: commuting to work, taking children to school and buying groceries while waiting for news from a city where loved ones may be facing security forces.

The smallest signs can provide comfort — a message marked as read, a familiar voice on a rushed call, a photograph sent without explanation.

But the fear quickly returns.

“When they say, ‘Don’t worry about us,’ that is when I worry the most,” **[NAME]** said. “All we can do is keep calling, keep speaking and hope they answer.”
